files.text:
A print like this began with a publisher. Nishimuraya Yohachi, who traded as Eijudō, bought the design from Hokusai, then past seventy, as one of a set of views of Mount Fuji, and paid for everything that followed. A clean copy of the drawing went to the carver, who pasted it face down on a plank of mountain cherry, sawn along the grain and planed smooth, rubbed the paper thin until the lines showed through from behind, and cut away everything that was not a line. The drawing was destroyed in the cutting. What survived was the key block: the picture in outline, standing a few millimetres proud of the wood.

From that block he pulled a handful of proofs, and on them the artist marked where each colour should go, one proof to a colour. Each was pasted on a fresh block and cut in turn: the red of the mountain, the sky, the forest and its trees, the shadow on the summit. Every block carried the same two small ridges in its margin, an L at one corner and a short straight stop along the bottom edge, so that a sheet laid against them would fall in the same place every time.

The printer worked at a low bench with the block in front of him and a stack of damp paper at his side. The paper was kōzo, made from the inner bark of the mulberry, sized with alum and glue and dampened the night before so that it would take the colour and hold its size. He brushed pigment onto the block with a little rice paste to give it body, laid a sheet against the marks, and rubbed its back with a baren, a coil of twisted bamboo cord in a shallow disc wrapped in a bamboo sheath, working it in small circles and zigzags across the block until the colour came through to the face. Then he peeled the sheet away, set it on the stack, and inked again. He printed the whole edition, perhaps two hundred sheets, from one block before he moved on to the next, the palest colours first and the darkest last.

The blue of the sky is graded by hand. Before each impression he wiped the inked block with a damp cloth so that the colour thinned toward the horizon; it is called bokashi, and because it was done again for every sheet, no two skies are quite the same. The blue itself was new. Prussian blue had only lately come to Edo in quantity, by way of the Chinese and Dutch ships at Nagasaki, and this series was among the first to make so much of it. Look closely at the red and you can see the grain of the cherry, printed with the colour.

A generation later, in the ninth month of 1857, the publisher Uoya Eikichi brought out this summer storm on the Ōhashi bridge as one of Hiroshige's hundred views of Edo; the two round seals in the upper margin are the censor's, giving the year and the month. Hiroshige was sixty and had a year to live. The rain is two blocks of fine lines, one black and one a shade paler, cut at slightly different angles so that the shower seems to come down in sheets. To print them the carver left every line standing alone, a ridge of cherry no wider than a hair, the whole height of the block.

The dark band across the top of the sky was wiped in sumi, as the blue was over Fuji, and under the bridge the pale river deepens into a second bokashi of Prussian blue. The series sold, and the blocks were inked and rubbed again and again for years after the first edition. Thirty years on, in Paris, Vincent van Gogh copied this print in oils and painted a border of characters around it, taken from other prints, that he could not read.

# woodblock-print A real Japanese colour woodblock print, printed in front of you as you scroll. The sheet starts as blank washi on the page, and the picture arrives the way it did in a printer's shop in Edo: the key block first, the outline in sumi, then each colour block in turn, palest first and darkest last. Every impression is rubbed in by a baren: for a moment the ink lies in swirled, uneven patches with the grain of the cherry block running through it, then a second pass evens it out. The block's relief is pressed into the paper, ink pools a little at the edges of shapes, and each block lands a pixel or two out of register and settles into the marks. Scroll back and the print un-prints. The demo prints Hokusai's *Red Fuji* (six blocks) and Hiroshige's *Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi* (twelve, ending with the two rain blocks). ```html
``` Or `import { woodblockPrint } from './woodblock-print.js'` and call `woodblockPrint(section, { src, mode, runway, margin, light })`; it returns `destroy()`. ## Options | attribute | option | default | what it does | |----------------|----------|------------|--------------| | `data-src` | `src` | required | The print's JSON: size, paper colour, and per block its ink (optical density at full coverage), bounding box and flags. | | `data-atlas` | `atlas` | `-blocks.webp` | The coverage maps, one greyscale strip (columns of layers if tall). | | `data-mode` | `mode` | `scroll` | `scroll`: a pinned stage on a runway, one impression per stretch of scroll. `static`: the finished print in the flow. | | `data-runway` | `runway` | `72` | Scroll length per impression, in svh (plus 90svh of lead-in and run-out). The Hiroshige uses `60`: it has twelve blocks. | | `data-margin` | `margin` | `.085` | Sheet margin as a fraction of the print's short side (the bottom margin is 1.55x, for the kento). The Hiroshige crop already carries its own margin and seals, so it uses `.035`. | | `data-light` | `light` | `pointer` | `pointer`: a raking light that swings toward a mouse over the sheet (touch leaves it alone). `fixed`: light from the upper left. | | `data-webgl` | `webgl` | `on` | `off` forces the 2D fallback (for testing). | Block flags in the JSON: `bokashi` (0-1, how strongly the wiping streaks of the cloth show in the graded part while it arrives) and `depth` (how deep the block presses into the paper; key defaults to 1.6, others 1). ## How it works **Separation (offline, Python).** The print is turned into optical density relative to its paper, `OD = -ln(I / paper)`, in the sRGB-encoded values (sRGB is close enough to a power law that products survive the encoding, so the shader can multiply encoded colours directly). In OD, inks add, and one ink at any strength is one direction: a bokashi is one block whose density varies, not a stack of blocks. - *Thin dark structures first.* A morphological top-hat (OD minus its grey opening with a 3px disc) isolates lines. Rain is found by rotating that map through 2-17° and opening along the vertical with a 61px line: long straight strokes survive; each stroke's median angle sorts it into one of the two rain blocks (they cut at about 6° and 12°). Short strokes with the same lean are caught by their shape (moments of each component). What is left that is thin and sumi-coloured is the key block; cartouche and signature boxes use a 6px disc so whole strokes come away. - *Broad fields.* The remainder is unmixed per pixel onto a small set of ink directions (Prussian blue and bengara red for Hokusai; sumi, two blues, yellow, red and green for Hiroshige), choosing the best single ink, pair or triple by non-negative least squares. Inks are allowed only where they belong (no red in Hiroshige's sky; paper toning outside the image is not ink). - *Blocks.* Each ink is split into the blocks a carver would cut: the same blue is the sky, the forest and the shadow on the summit; the same sumi is the dusk bokashi, the far shore and the piers. Region weights are feathered, so the split never shows in the composite. Each block's ink vector is then refit by least squares (others held), three rounds. - The composite of all blocks on the paper reproduces the original to a mean error of about 3.7/255 after webp encoding (1.6 before, for Hiroshige). Blocks are normalised to their 99.95th percentile and saved as one greyscale webp strip; the JSON holds each block's ink at full coverage. **Printing order.** Key first, as Edo printers did it: the outline goes down on the clean sheet and every colour block, cut from proofs of it, registers to it. It also reads best here: a drawing appears, then colour fills it. Then light to dark: yellow, red, green, the pale river, the sky tint, the far shore, the piers, the deep water, the sumi dusk, and the rain last. **Front end.** One quad, one fragment shader (generated for the number of blocks): coverage for up to 12 blocks in three RGBA textures, packed on load from the strip at about the displayed resolution (so no mipmaps are needed and nothing aliases on a phone). Per pixel: `paper × exp(-Σ coverage × density × ink)`. - *The baren.* Pressure reaches each part of the block in turn, roughly top to bottom and across, with the hand's unevenness in it (two scales of low-frequency noise), so the front is a wide, ragged band and never a shape. Where it has reached, the ink is taken fibre by fibre: a paper-tooth map (fine speckle plus the kozo fibres) is thresholded against the pressure, so the partial state is goma-zuri, a crisp speckle of bare flecks that fills in as the density rises. Faint baren tracks (thin, irregular loops along the rows) press a little harder where they pass and show only as slightly denser speckle inside the printed area. - *Wood grain.* Fine, slightly wavy parallel lines (period at least 3 CSS px, so nothing aliases on a phone), drawn crisp: they take the ink first while it is thin and stay as a whisper once it is full (the original's own grain is in the coverage maps). - *Bokashi.* Graded blocks carry the horizontal streaks of the wiping cloth in their mid-tones while they arrive. - *Pooling.* Coverage minus its 4-tap neighbourhood adds a slightly darker rim inside every edge, a little stronger while the ink is wet. - *Emboss.* Each printed block's footprint is a depression in the paper; its gradient (the same four taps) is lit from the upper left, or from the pointer's side. The kento (an L-shaped kagi at the lower left and a straight hikitsuke along the bottom) are blind grooves in the bottom margin, pressed with the first impression. - *Misregistration.* The block being printed is sampled from an offset of one or two CSS pixels that settles to zero over the first three quarters of its impression. - *Paper.* A 1024² tileable texture made once in JS: long kozo fibres (curved strokes, mostly lighter), formation clouds, fine grain, and the wood streaks. The deckle wanders a little at two scales, thins and turns translucent in its last few pixels, with loose fibres beyond it; the shadow is faint and tight. The sheet is a few percent darker (damp) until the last impression is done. - Scroll is followed on a critically damped spring, so a fast flick still shows the print being made and nothing overshoots. ## Theming | variable | default | used for | |--------------|--------------------------|----------| | `--paper` | `#f3f0e8` | the page around the sheet | | `--wb-runway`| set by the script | section height in scroll mode | | `--gutter` | `clamp(16px, 3vw, 32px)` | side padding of the stage | The sheet takes the print's own paper colour from its JSON (the aged cream of the impression), so the finished print matches the original. ## Making a new print Scripts live outside the component (the separation is per print and needs looking at). The recipe: crop inside the sheet, resize to ~2000px on the long side, take paper from the brightest unprinted area, sample a few pure patches for the ink directions, check the residual of a pair/triple unmix (anything large means a missing ink), cut blocks by region, refit, then view every block alone and the reconstruction beside the original at full size before exporting. ## Accessibility and motion - Without JS (or if loading fails) the original print stays as an `` dressed as a sheet; the canvas is `aria-hidden`. The art is ornament (`alt=""`), credits are in `assets/credits.json`. - Reduced motion: no runway; the finished print, still. The raking light still follows a mouse (direct manipulation). - Phone: the stage fits the width; everything is driven by scroll; the canvas is `touch-action: pan-y`, so a vertical swipe always scrolls. ## Cost - Assets: Red Fuji 1.1 MB of blocks + 0.6 MB fallback; Sudden Shower 2.3 MB + 0.8 MB. Packing on load: one `getImageData` per block at display size. - A frame draws only while the scroll spring or the light is moving and the section is on screen (IntersectionObserver); nothing runs when idle or in a hidden tab. DPR capped at 2. The baren's loop only runs for the one block being printed; finished blocks cost ~5 texture reads each, shared noise included. - Without WebGL, a 2D canvas multiplies each block in as a still layer (`exp(-c × ink)` baked per block) and fades it in with the scroll. ## Credits Both prints: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0). Katsushika Hokusai, *South Wind, Clear Sky* (Red Fuji), ca. 1830–32, JP2960; Utagawa Hiroshige, *Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake*, 1857, JP2522. The block separations are ours. See `assets/credits.json`. No third-party code.
